title: Medium exam 9
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace a few steps: letter case in names, pipeline statuses, aliases, read, directory permissions, systemd defaults, exit codes, startup files, wc and background PIDs.

questions.title: Case and file names
questions.text: Which statement about upper and lower case in Linux is FALSE?

options.t: `README` and `readme` can exist side by side in the same directory.
options.why: True: they are different names.
True: names are case sensitive.

options.t: `Echo hi` fails with "command not found", while `echo hi` works.
options.why: True: command names are case sensitive too.

options.t: If `Notes.txt` exists, `touch notes.txt` only updates the time of that file.
options.why: False: `notes.txt` is another name, so `touch` creates a second, empty file.

questions.title: Status of a group
questions.text: You type `(cd /tmp; false); echo $?`. What is printed?

options.why: The status of a parenthesised group is the status of its last command, and `false` returns 1.
`cd /tmp` succeeded, but it is not the last command of the group.
`echo $?` prints a status number; nothing in the line prints the directory.
127 means "command not found", and both `cd` and `false` exist.

questions.title: Redefining an alias
questions.text: In an interactive shell you type `alias ll='ls -l'`, then `alias ll='ls -la'`, then `alias ll`. What does the last command print?

options.why: Defining an alias again replaces the previous definition, and `alias name` shows the current one.
The second definition replaced the first one.

options.t: Both definitions, one after the other.
options.why: An alias has only one value at a time.
`alias ll` prints the definition in the form `alias name='...'`, it does not run it.

questions.title: Two ways of reading
questions.text: Compare `read -p "Name: " n` and `read -t 5 n`. Which statement is correct?

options.t: The first shows a prompt; the second waits at most 5 seconds and then fails.
options.why: `-p` gives a prompt text and `-t` a timeout in seconds; on a timeout `read` returns a non-zero status.

options.t: The first waits 5 seconds and the second shows a prompt.
options.why: The options are the other way round.

options.t: Both wait for ever, since the options only change how the variable is stored.
options.why: `-t` is exactly what limits the waiting time.

options.t: The second reads from a file called `5` into `n`.
options.why: `-t` takes the timeout as its argument; `read` still reads standard input.

questions.title: Listing needs read
questions.text: Which statement about the permissions of a directory is FALSE?

options.t: To create a file in it you need write and execute permission on it.
options.why: True: creating adds a name to the directory.

options.t: To rename a file in it you need write and execute permission on it.
options.why: True: renaming changes a name stored in the directory.

options.t: With only read permission you can list the names, but you cannot get the details of the files.
options.why: True: `ls` shows the names, while `ls -l` answers "Permission denied" for each entry.

options.t: With only execute permission you can list its names with `ls`.
options.why: False: listing needs read permission. With only `x` you can pass through the directory to a file whose name you already know.

questions.title: A text-only default
questions.text: You want the next boots of a systemd machine to start in text mode, without the graphical desktop. Which command does that?

options.why: It changes the default target for the following boots.
It switches the running system to that target now, but the default for the next boot does not change.
It is the graphical target that gives the desktop.
`get-default` only prints the current default and takes no argument.

questions.title: A command that does not exist
questions.text: You type `foo`, which is not a builtin, an alias or a program in the `PATH`. What does `echo $?` print right after?

options.why: The shell uses 127 for "command not found" (126 is for a file that exists but cannot be executed).
Status 0 means success, and the command did not run.
1 is the generic failure status of many commands, not the one the shell reports for a missing command.
2 is used by many commands for incorrect usage; it is not the status of a missing command.

options.t: `~/.profile` is for login shells; `~/.bashrc` is for interactive shells that are not login shells.
options.why: Many `.profile` files include `~/.bashrc`, so that both kinds of shell get the same aliases.

options.t: `~/.bashrc` is read only at login and `~/.profile` by every new terminal window you open.
options.why: It is the other way round.
Every user has them in the home directory.

options.t: `~/.profile` configures the kernel and `~/.bashrc` configures the boot loader.
options.why: Both are shell startup files.

questions.title: Counting entries
questions.text: The directory `e` contains two files, `a` and `b`. Which command prints just the number of entries of `e`, `2`?

options.why: `ls` prints one name per line when its output is a pipe, and `wc -l` counts the lines.
The long listing starts with a line `total ...`, so it prints `3`.
`wc` would try to read `e` as a file, and it is a directory.
Without the pipe `ls` receives `wc` and `-l` as more arguments.

questions.title: The PID of a background job
questions.text: Which line starts `sleep 30` in the background and then prints its PID?

options.why: `$!` is the PID of the last background job.
`;` runs `sleep` in the foreground: the `echo` waits 30 seconds, and `$!` is empty because nothing was run in the background.
`$$` is the PID of the shell itself, not of the background job.
The `echo` runs after `sleep` ends, and `$!` is empty if no background job was started.
